newsitem.title: UK: Card Clear joins fight against Net fraud.
newsitem.headline: Card Clear joins fight against Net fraud.

text.p: British card payment and fraud prevention service Card Clear Plc said on Monday it was setting up a security service for the Internet to help users identify each other and fight fraud.

Interactive shopping and banking have exploded on the Internet, with Visa credit card transactions rising at 450 percent per annum, but most consumers are still wary of putting money where their keyboard is, Card Clear said.

"The main problem with the Internet is making sure both parties are aware who they dealing with, particularly when they have to hand over credit card details," finance director Oliver Cooke told Reuters in a telephone interview.

Card Clear is planning to offer electronic security certificates to Internet users which would guarantee the person at your website was genuine -- a service expanding in the U.S. but currently unavailable in Britain, the company said.

"Let's say you were a Harrods customer. You'd be reasonably well-off and linked to the Internet. You would also be an obvious target for someone who wanted to rip off your credit card...You would really want to know if you were actually connected to Harrods on-line," Cooke said.

Card Clear said Internet revenue was set to explode to $73 billion by 2000 from around $1.1 billion last year. It said half of all credit card transactions would be on the Internet by 2005 but expansion was being limited by worries about security.

Cooke said the certificates would ease dealings between users and also help prevent retailers and companies being defrauded by individuals. Other uses include the protected transfer of confidential documents.

Under the system, Cooke said individuals or companies would apply for the certificates, priced at 10-12 stg ($16.30-$19.60) each, and provide personal details which would be verified by a third party, such as a solicitor.

"We would then do a certain level of accreditation and issue a coded certification...we can say, we have checked out this party and they are who they claim to be. It's not expensive but would give enormous peace of mind," Cooke said.

He said Card Clear, which is operating the certification under the name Inter Clear as a joint venture with JCP Computer Services, would make regular checks on holders. Inter Clear would also maintain a blacklist of compromised certificates if, for example, a stolen credit card had been used.

Card Clear's foray into electronic certification follows VeriSign Inc. in the U.S. which took the Secure Electronics Transations (SET) standard developed by Visa and Mastercard and started electronic distribution of digital identification.
Cooke said his company, listed on London's Alternative Investment Market, was looking at the SET standard.
He said it was difficult to estimate possible demand for such a fledgling market but Card Clear was likely to restrict its business to the British market.

Card Clear, based in Woking, southern England, said it already had strong ties with credit card issuers and banks. Annual turnover totals between six and seven million stg and market capitalisation was around 40 million, Cooke said. ($ = 0.612 British Pounds Sterling)
